articles.title: Rochdale AFC Secures 1-0 Victory Against Swindon Town
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC clinched a late 1-0 win over Swindon Town at the Crown Oil Arena, capitalising on a red card for the visitors.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC achieved a crucial 1-0 victory against Swindon Town in a League Two match held at the Crown Oil Arena on Saturday, October 3, 2026. The decisive moment came late in the game when Cian Hayes scored the only goal, taking advantage of Swindon's reduced numbers after Kaelan Majekodunmi received a second yellow card in the 85th minute.

The match started with both teams struggling to create clear chances, with neither goalkeeper facing significant threats in the first half. However, the game shifted dramatically following the red card for Swindon, which allowed Rochdale to press for a winner. Just three minutes after the dismissal, Hayes found the net, glancing home a header from a knock-on by Aden Flint, securing all three points for the home side.

This victory marks an important turnaround for Rochdale, who have now taken seven points from their last three matches, including two consecutive wins. The result puts additional pressure on Swindon Town's manager Ian Holloway, who had described himself as a "dead man walking" prior to the match, as his team continues to struggle in the league.

Looking ahead, Rochdale will aim to build on this momentum in their upcoming fixtures, while Swindon will need to regroup quickly to avoid further setbacks in their campaign.

articles.title: Middleton Oktoberfest Celebrations Attract Hundreds of Visitors
articles.excerpt: Middleton's Oktoberfest celebrations drew large crowds over the weekend, featuring entertainment, food, and activities for all ages in Middleton Gardens.
articles.content_html:
Middleton's Oktoberfest celebrations took place over the weekend, attracting hundreds of visitors to the town centre. The two-day festival, hosted by the Rochdale Development Agency, Rochdale Council, the Britannia Inn, Middleton Township, and Middleton Co-operating, featured a variety of entertainment and activities for attendees of all ages.

On Saturday, the festivities kicked off with performances from the Middleton Popstars Academy and the Conker Championships. Musical acts included Big Swingy Thing and acoustic guitarist Ben Floyd, providing a lively atmosphere throughout the day. The evening entertainment featured psychedelic rock band Innafield and local band Lazarus, drawing in a crowd eager to enjoy the music.

Sunday's events began with traditional oompah tunes from the Parpundales, also known as the Middleton Band, starting at 1pm. This set the tone for a day filled with Oktoberfest spirit, as families and friends gathered to celebrate together in Middleton Gardens.

The success of the Oktoberfest celebrations highlights the community's enthusiasm for local events and the importance of such gatherings in fostering community spirit. Further details on upcoming events in Middleton can be found on the Rochdale Council website.

articles.title: New Gas Governor Proposed for Middleton to Address Network Pressure
articles.excerpt: Cadent Gas Ltd has submitted plans to install a new gas governor in Middleton to alleviate pressure on the local gas network, following high demand from residents and businesses.
articles.content_html:
Cadent Gas Ltd has applied to Rochdale Council for permission to install a new gas governor, kiosk, and fencing next to 56 Bonscale Crescent in Middleton. The proposed installation aims to address the current pressure on the existing gas network in the area, which has been struggling to meet high demand from both residential and commercial users.

The application, submitted by MacMarshalls Rural Chartered Surveyors & Planning Consultants, indicates that the new gas governor is essential for the safe distribution of gas. It will control gas pressure, reducing it from high to low to ensure a reliable supply for local residents and businesses. The proposed kiosk will be located in a corner of an open space that includes a children's play area, closest to the road and adjacent to the boundary of the property at 56 Bonscale Crescent.

Previously, there was a plan to install the kiosk beside 54 Bonscale Crescent, but that application was withdrawn. The new proposal is seen as a necessary step to cope with the increasing gas usage in the locality, which has made the installation of a new governor imperative.

The kiosk itself, measuring 26.8 cubic metres, falls within permitted development parameters and does not require planning permission as a standalone structure. The council is expected to review the application in the coming weeks, and if approved, the installation could significantly improve gas supply reliability in the area.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: A look at how a hollowed pool under the viaduct became the Fairies’ Chapel — and where documented history ends and local legend begins.
articles.summary: A look at how a hollowed pool under the viaduct became the Fairies’ Chapel — and where documented history ends and local legend begins.
articles.body:
Healey Dell is one of the borough’s best‑known beauty spots: a wooded cleft carved by the River Spodden, ringed by mill ruins and spanned by a dramatic 19th‑century viaduct. The site is a managed nature reserve with a heritage centre and family trails; Rochdale Borough Council describes the area’s waterfalls, industrial archaeology and a “Fairy Grotto” aimed at visitors and school groups. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The viaduct that dominates the Dell is a real, verifiable landmark. It was built for the Lancashire & Yorkshire extension railway in 1869–70 and is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England (listing first entered 30 November 1984). That listing records the viaduct’s construction, materials and form — part of the industrial story that shaped the valley. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

The feature usually called the Fairies’ Chapel is not a chapel in the ecclesiastical sense but a pulpit‑like rock niche and pool in a narrow gorge the Dell team calls “the Thrutch.” Local interpretation and geological description agree that river erosion, and later changes caused by a notorious storm in July 1838, explain the hollowed rock and the loss of any larger cavernous spaces once observed by Victorian visitors. In short: the “chapel” is a natural feature shaped by water and weather, not a carved church interior. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

That said, the Fairies’ Chapel inherits a long local storytelling tradition. Many of the tales printed and retold about Healey Dell in the 19th century come from collectors such as John Roby whose Traditions of Lancashire (early 1830s) gathered regional stories about fairies, witches and other wonders. Those collected tales — literary and folkloric material rather than archival records — are the root of the Dell’s supernatural reputation. Roby and later local poets offered dramatic episodes: fairy courts, prophecies, a “Healey Dwarf” figure and stories in which a Fairy King or Queen interacts with local people. These are stories recorded as folklore, not documentary history. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c1/Lancashire_legends_%28IA_lancashirelegend00roby%29.pdf))

Where folklore ends and documented fact begins is important to underline. There are no contemporary legal records, parish registers, court documents or archaeological reports that verify the presence of supernatural beings. The town and landscape histories, council information and Historic England’s listing describe the Dell’s topography, industrial past and later conservation; they do not and cannot confirm fairy visitations. When modern guides and the heritage centre tell the tales, they are continuing a living local tradition — useful for storytelling, education and tourism — but not replacing historical evidence. If a claim cannot be verified in the records, it should be treated as folklore. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

For visitors today the best approach is twofold: bring curiosity and common sense. Enjoy the pulpit‑shaped niche, the tumbling river, the ruins and the view from the viaduct — those are physical realities documented by authorities and listed records. Enjoy, too, the older printed tales and the heritage centre’s retellings: they are part of local cultural history, showing how people have used landscape to shape stories about identity and wonder. If you’re hoping to meet a Fairy King, leave room for imagination — but don’t mistake a good story for an archive entry.

If you want to read further: Rochdale Borough Council’s Healey Dell page sets out the reserve’s facilities and modern management; Historic England holds the official listing for the viaduct; and 19th‑century collections of Lancashire legends (for example Roby’s Traditions) show how the fairy stories entered print and public imagination. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

articles.title: Heybrook Primary and Nursery School Celebrates Second Eco-Schools Award
articles.excerpt: Heybrook Primary and Nursery School in Rochdale has achieved its second Eco-Schools Award, marking its commitment to environmental education and sustainability with a community planting event.
articles.content_html:
Heybrook Primary and Nursery School has celebrated the achievement of its second Eco-Schools Award, recognising its commitment to environmental education and sustainability. The award highlights the school's ongoing efforts to empower students to make a positive impact on the environment through sustainable practices.

To commemorate this significant milestone, pupils, staff, and families gathered to plant 1,000 spring bulbs across the school grounds. This community planting event welcomed parents and grandparents, allowing them to work alongside children to create vibrant displays that will enhance the school's environment and support local biodiversity.

The Eco-Schools Award is designed to encourage schools to integrate sustainability into their curriculum and promote environmental awareness among students. Headteacher Toni Moore expressed pride in the school's accomplishment, stating, "We are incredibly proud to have received our second Eco-Schools Award."

The planting of the bulbs not only beautifies the school grounds but also reinforces the school's commitment to fostering environmentally responsible citizens. The school community looks forward to seeing the colourful displays in the coming months, which will serve as a reminder of their dedication to sustainability.
